The only points path to nonstop business class service to French Polynesia.

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Champagne in hand, watching the sun melt into the ocean from 35,000 feet. In eight hours, you'll land in Papeete — French Polynesia's gateway to overwater bungalows, turquoise lagoons, and the kind of trip people save their whole lives for. And you got here on points. This is the Air France business class seat to Tahiti, and it represents one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. Not just because of where you're going — though Tahiti is bucket-list by definition — but because of the staggering gap between what you'd pay in cash and what you'll pay in miles. **The math will genuinely stop you in your tracks.** A business class ticket from Los Angeles (LAX) to Papeete (PPT) on Air France regularly retails between **$5,000 and $12,000 per person**. That's the cash reality. But with Flying Blue miles — Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program — you can book the same seat for as few as **88,000 miles**. At the high end of retail pricing, that's a value of **13.6 cents per point (CPP)**. Even at the low end, you're extracting **5.7 CPP** from miles that most programs value at 1–2 cents. In the ChooseFI community, we talk constantly about optimizing every dollar toward financial independence — and a redemption that turns 88,000 transferable points into a $5,000–$12,000 experience is about as powerful as it gets. Here's what makes this feel different from your average business class booking: Air France operates a **Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner** on this route, featuring a modern, premium business class cabin with direct aisle access for every seat, noise-reducing windows, better humidity levels, and that unmistakably French touch in service and catering. You're not just flying in a recliner — you're flying in a genuine lie-flat pod on one of aviation's most celebrated aircraft. And this is the only nonstop option. Air France is the **sole carrier operating nonstop LAX–PPT** service. That's not a coincidence — it's a pricing inefficiency baked into the route's geography, and it's exactly the kind of structural advantage the ChooseFI community knows how to exploit.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program is the only way to book the only nonstop flight between Los Angeles and Tahiti using points — and that program happens to offer some of the most generous award pricing in the world.

In a recent development, flying Blue uses a dynamic award pricing model, meaning costs fluctuate based on demand and availability. That sounds like a disadvantage — and sometimes it is. But here's the inefficiency: Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards every single month. These are fixed-price award seats on select routes, discounted 25–50% off standard award pricing. When Tahiti appears as a Promo Reward destination (which it does periodically), the pricing drops dramatically — and crucially, Promo Reward tickets eliminate carrier-imposed fuel surcharges entirely.

In a recent development, fuel surcharges on Air France-operated flights are normally moderate, but they're real — they can add $200–$500 to an award ticket. Promo Rewards wipe those out. This is the pricing inefficiency: Flying Blue is essentially subsidizing this cabin to drive demand, and you can capture the subsidy.

Choose a Buyer’s Agent Before You Tour – Interview Three, Then Negotiate the Fee

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (420 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Interview at least three buyer’s agents, and negotiate the written agreement with the one you pick before you tour a single home.
  • Recent findings suggest that unless the seller agrees to cover it, you pay the fee that agreement sets.
  • In a recent development, there’s no standard fee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Interview at least three buyer’s agents, and negotiate the written agreement with the one you pick before you tour a single home. That agreement sets your agent’s pay, how long you’re committed, and what it takes to get out, and agents now ask for your signature before any showing.

Recent findings suggest that unless the seller agrees to cover it, you pay the fee that agreement sets. The time to bargain over it is before you sign, while the next agent on your list is still an option.

In a recent development, there’s no standard fee. Under National Association of Realtors rules in force since August 2024, the agreement must state the fee as a set amount or rate, never as whatever the seller happens to offer. The agent can’t collect more than that from anyone, the seller included, and the agreement must say that commissions aren’t set by law and are negotiable.

Redfin’s sales data put the average buyer’s agent commission at 2.42% of the price in the third quarter of 2025, so an agent who opens at 3% is asking above that average.

In a recent development, get names from friends who recently bought homes, then pick three agents who can name several homes they helped buyers close on in your neighborhood and price range in the past year. Ask each how they’d handle a bidding war, an inspection that turns up problems, and a lender’s appraisal that values the home below your offer.

Read each one’s agreement, then negotiate these terms with the one you choose:.

Once you sign, tell your agent your real budget, share your preapproval letter showing how much you can borrow, and name the features you won’t give up. Before every offer, ask for recent sales of similar homes nearby.

Picture a buyer shopping for a $400,000 home who passes on the first agent’s six-month agreement at 3%, a $12,000 fee, and signs with the third for 60 days at 2.25%, or $9,000, which is $3,000 less.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

Decorate Your Wedding for Less – Pick a Pretty Venue and Reuse the Ceremony Pieces

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (468 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The cheapest wedding decorations are the ones you never buy or rent.
  • Decor costs climb with every rental and every craft-store run, and a plain room takes more of both to look like a wedding.
  • According to recent reports, A garden, a historic building, or a hall with good lighting and its own linens needs little decor, and anything the venue includes is one less thing to rent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The cheapest wedding decorations are the ones you never buy or rent. Book a venue that looks good on its own and ask what it includes. Then move your ceremony arch, aisle decorations, and signs to the reception, and borrow or buy secondhand before you rent anything.

Decor costs climb with every rental and every craft-store run, and a plain room takes more of both to look like a wedding.

According to recent reports, A garden, a historic building, or a hall with good lighting and its own linens needs little decor, and anything the venue includes is one less thing to rent. Every piece you do bring can serve the ceremony and then the reception for one price.

Recent findings suggest that for whatever is still missing, borrow first, buy secondhand next, and rent last. Say a rental shop quotes $1,200 for an arch, aisle lanterns, signs, and table runners. Borrow the lanterns from friends and buy a recent couple’s arch, signs, and runners for $300, and you pay $900 less than the $1,200 quote, though you’ll haul and set up the pieces yourself.

Before you sign with a venue, ask for its list of what comes with the room, such as linens, candle holders, easels, or string lights. Ask for its rules on candles and setup times, too. Many venues allow candles only inside glass that rises above the flame, and two hours of setup time rules out decor that takes all afternoon to put together.

Sources indicate that then proposal where each ceremony piece goes at the reception: the arch behind the head table, the aisle lanterns along the bar, and the welcome sign at the door. Ask a friend to move them during cocktail hour, while you’re taking photos.

Couples sell the decor they used once they’re married, so search Facebook Marketplace and local wedding resale groups for the pieces on your list, and sell yours there afterward. Light the reception with string lights and candles in place of extra flowers. Skip any do-it-yourself project whose supplies cost about as much as renting the finished piece, since you’d put in the hours and save nothing.

On your wedding-day schedule, list each piece that moves and the friend moving it, so the arch is behind the head table before your guests sit down.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

#56539. Breaking: $656,000 of Frugal Things I Still Love Doing

📅 24 Jul 2024 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1986 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: $656,000 of Frugal Things I Still Love Doing

📅 24 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Until he got all rich and fancy so that he no longer understands the common person’s plight.
  • Stash probably doesn’t even practice any of these money-saving things he preaches any more!”.
  • According to recent reports, when I read things like this, I can’t help but laugh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I used to read Mr. Money Mustache”,.

“Until he got all rich and fancy so that he no longer understands the common person’s plight.

Stash probably doesn’t even practice any of these money-saving things he preaches any more!”.

According to recent reports, when I read things like this, I can’t help but laugh. Because on the one hand, when you put a bunch of personal life details online like this, being misunderstood is just part of the package. But on the other hand, if the critics could peek in and see our real lives – not just mine but those of all the Mustachians – they would have to give up their conspiracy theories and accept the fact that this stuff just works.

It has been revealed that because really, not much has changed when it comes to the basics. Like many MMM readers over the past twelve years, my total wealth level has increased pretty regularly. But also like many of us, I haven’t felt the need to change very much about my spending because I was doing my best to live an enjoyable life in the first place.

According to recent reports, how have so many people found such great success? I think we Mustachians have something that’s a bit more rare and special than standard financial advice, which is what makes it work so well:.

It has been revealed that standard Advice: Slash your spending and make sacrifices until you reach a certain savings percentage, and beyond that it doesn’t matter, it’s all personal choice. More income? Great, that means you don’t have to sacrifice as much! FatFIRE for everyone!

Sources indicate that mustachianism: Cultivate a love of efficiency, creativity, self awareness, and self improvement. Use this knowledge to improve your life in all ways, including those which help you live better even as your monthly expense rate drops over time.

So what does this mean in practice?

Industry observers note that well, I’ll give you some examples from my own present-day life. Things I do because I happen to enjoy them, which also happen to save a lot of money. Some of these are normal, some are silly and may end up in some future gossip magazine hit piece, but all of them happen to work for me, so the critics can be damned.

Recent findings suggest that as I list each item, I’ll include an estimate of how much the activity saves me per decade, because you should always think at least in terms of decades. To make that calculation yourself, just use the “rule of 172” – take a monthly expense and multiply it by 172 to estimate how much it would compound into over ten years, if invested.

1) Fixing my own House (and everybody else’s too).

Industry observers note that I’m a massive believer in self-sufficiency, and working to build up the skills to manage the most key parts of your own life without depending on too many things (or people) that are outside of your control. In other words, one giant recipe for a happy life is simply to Become a Producer of the Things You Most Enjoy Consuming.

In a recent development, and in my case, I happen to love houses. I like living in beautiful, functional spaces and sharing them with friends. But most houses are ugly and poorly designed when you buy them, so I realized that I also love solving problems and redesigning old buildings to become upcoming again. I enjoy this process so much that I spend most of my free time doing it – on both my own properties and the homes of friends.

Industry observers note that and I love teaching other people to gain power over their own houses too. It’s amazing how great people feel as they lose their fear and dependence on outside contractors, and gain the ability to fix and maintain things with their own two hands.

Savings: An average of $20,000 per year = $287,000 per decade.

You know what’s great? Having so much money that you can buy whatever you want – high quality things which get delivered to your front door the very next day.

You know what’s even better? Not buying some of those newly introduced things, and instead finding ways to share, repurpose and buy equally high quality items from other people who don’t need them any more. All while building up your own community and creating new friendships in the process.

Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, and even NextDoor all have Buy Nothing groups for most areas. In the MMM-HQ community, we run a Discord server with about 200 local people, who chat around the clock on a wide range of subjects. They help each other with major projects in one channel called #diyhowto, and give away and sell things on #forsale and #buynothing.

Although our private Discord group is my favorite, I also use Craigslist regularly, and probably save (and earn) a few thousand every year thanks to the habit:.

Savings: About $42,000 per decade.

Sources indicate that we all know that Mr. Money Mustache’s biggest contribution to personal finance is to insist that bike transportation is the best way to get around. And I still feel this way. As we learned in The True Cost of Commuting, cars cost at least 50 cents per mile to operate, while bikes are much cheaper, mainly due to reduced depreciation and maintenance costs (which are even bigger than the gas savings).

Industry observers note that I do still use bikes (or walking) for at least 95% of my local trips these days, but because I live in the center of a small city, my life is pretty local. So this still only adds up to about 2000 miles per year, a savings of “only” $14,000 per decade.

According to recent reports, but when you choose active transportation, there’s much more to the picture than just cutting your car expenses. You’re changing everything about your physical and mental health picture for the better, which brings us to the next point of….

Although I’m no competitive athlete, whenever I see an option to make my body work a bit harder, I usually take it. Stairs instead of elevators, running the golf course instead of using a golf cart, moving my own furniture and appliances instead of calling a mover, shoveling snow and raking leaves instead of using a machine.

When I face a decision like this, I simply ask myself the question: “Well, Mustache. Do you want MORE health and fitness, or LESS?” Putting it in that context makes the answer obvious. Every bit helps, because when it comes to your body, the rule is pretty much use it or lose it.

But how much money does this save? There’s no real way to calculate it exactly, but I like to think of it this way: The US average health care spending is about $13,000 per person per year. My lifetime costs due to illness or medication so far have been just about zero, plus I know I’ve had more energy and greater productivity due to being healthy. Let’s just put it very conservatively and set the estimated savings and benefits at $10k per year which means.

Estimated Savings:  $140,000 per decade.

5) Saving Energy by Running my home like a Glamping Retreat.

Here’s where things get a bit silly, but my level of joy is actually at its greatest.

My personality type is probably a weird combination of an engineer, a carpenter, an artsy hippie, and a mad scientist. Oh, and a devoted homebody too. Because of this, my favorite activity most days is to just run around my house taking care of things and trying new little experiments and improvements.

Sometimes I’ll cut a few massive holes on on the South side of the house and install sliding doors and big windows to allow nice sunbeams and passive solar energy to get into my house and give me free heat in the winters. Other times it’s just smaller things to save energy and live more at at one with the seasons of my area:.

It has been revealed that even taken all together, these things are pretty small – the average combined gas and electric bill for my area is about $250 per month, while my usage adds up to about $75. So while we’re only saving about $30,000 per decade for what sounds like a lot of work to most people, I consider this to be the biggest win because I enjoy living in “MMM’s Energy Efficiency Playground” so much.

6) Local Living over Constant Travel.

“Hey, we’re having a big back yard pool party next weekend to celebrate Amy’s graduation from kindergarten, can you make it?”.

“OH NOOOO!!! We will be off in at Disneyland that whole week! We planned the trip months ago, I wish we could make it!

As I type this in the height of the summer season, I really feel this effect at its fullest: almost all of my friends are off on trips, and my guest suite here at home is almost constantly full. People are traveling a lot, and many of them sound like they wish they could spend a few more of their precious summer weeks and weekends at home.

In a recent development, I’ll let you in on a little secret: you can! The trick is saying, “no thanks” more often to plans that involve you being away, and “yes please” to things that let you stay at home. The benefits are numerous:.

Estimated Savings: Even if you replace just two weeks of travel for a family of four, with equivalent time at home you might save $5,000 per year in direct costs and a further $5,000 per year in incidental benefits like the health and local friendships. This would work out to a shocking $143,000 per decade of wealth increase!

Sources indicate that of course, travel is generally a good thing for broadening the life experience of you and your kids. It’s worth spending on, lavishly at times. But the key is to balance it out and be discerning, keeping the most enriching trips and pruning a few off the bottom of the list. And remembering that home time is valuable and healthy too.

And Whoa! We’ve already built up a huge list and I feel like I was just getting started.

Taken all together, we’ve already detailed things that compound to $656,000 every decade, which already more than double the median wealth that most American seniors have as they cruise nervously into their retirement years – after over 40 years of work!

In a recent development, and now that I’ve been writing this blog for over ten years myself, I can safely say that over $656,000 of even my most recent worth increases are directly attributable to these simple habits. The same ones many of us have been enjoying and preaching about all along, both before and after our retirement dates.

Sources indicate that if money is in genuinely short supply, you could go a lot further than the examples in this article. And indeed, there’s a lot more laid out in this blog or the MMM Boot Camp email series.

But one of the points of Mustachianism is that you usually don’t have to try all that hard. Just tweaking your lifestyle to be slightly less ridiculous and more efficient than average is usually all it takes.

Industry observers note that in the comments: what are your quirks and frugal indulgences? The things you do now to save money, or things you still do even after it’s no longer about the money? I often wonder how widespread this frugality-just-for-fun is. But since we Humans are a naturally curious and problem solving species in our natural state, I suspect there are many more of us out there.

Latest Update: Stop Porch Theft – Route Packages to a Locker or Pickup Counter for Free

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (372 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, package thieves can’t take a box that never sits on your porch.
  • Industry observers note that A $300 order left at your door at 10 a.m.
  • Amazon offers lockers at checkout, and UPS, FedEx, and USPS each let you send a box to a pickup point through a free online account.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, package thieves can’t take a box that never sits on your porch. Have your orders held at a locker, a store’s pickup counter, or your Post Office. Choose the pickup point at checkout or in each carrier’s free online account. For boxes that still come home, tell the driver where to leave them out of sight.

Industry observers note that A $300 order left at your door at 10 a.m. sits in view of the street until you get home from work. Sent to a locker two blocks away, the same box waits locked up until you collect it.

You can make that switch yourself. Amazon offers lockers at checkout, and UPS, FedEx, and USPS each let you send a box to a pickup point through a free online account.

UPS and FedEx pickup locations hold a box up to seven days. When a box has to come home, each carrier’s free account lets you tell the driver where to leave it, such as a side door or your building’s office. FedEx also delivers between 5 and 8 p.m. for $5.55 a package.

Report a stolen box to the seller right away. UPS pays claims to the shipper, not to you, so the seller is the one who can replace or refund the order. Then check the card you paid with for purchase protection, which can cover a stolen purchase.

Recent findings suggest that set the UPS preference once, and redirect each FedEx or USPS box the day its tracking number arrives. USPS refuses Delivery Instructions for a package already out for delivery, and FedEx says a box redirected by midnight the day before delivery should be ready for pickup on delivery day.

Match Your Side Income to What You Have Most – Money, Time, or a Skill

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, side income runs on money, time, or a skill, so build yours on the one you have the most of.
  • A side hustle picked because it’s popular can take the only two evenings you had free, or tie up savings you’ll need next year in a rental.
  • What you have to spare is the better guide, since money, time, and skill each pay in their own way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, side income runs on money, time, or a skill, so build yours on the one you have the most of. Spare savings can earn passive income, free hours suit gig work, and a skill clients pay for usually brings the highest hourly pay. Then invest part of what your side income earns.

A side hustle picked because it’s popular can take the only two evenings you had free, or tie up savings you’ll need next year in a rental.

What you have to spare is the better guide, since money, time, and skill each pay in their own way. Money earns income on what you put in, but you can also lose what you put in. Time pays by the hour or the task, and the pay stops when you stop. Selling a skill also takes your hours, but you set the rate, so it pays more per hour than gig work when few people can do the job.

Say a software tester with a packed schedule has 10 spare hours a month. She’s short on time but has a skill clients pay for, so she skips gig driving and takes two five-hour freelance testing projects at $50 an hour, which bring in $500 a month.

It has been revealed that savings you won’t need for years can earn passive income from dividend stocks, bond funds, a rental property, or a stake in a small business. Stocks and bond funds can fall in value, a rental brings vacancies and repairs, and a business stake can be lost entirely.

A skill sells as freelance work, tutoring, or consulting, and a freelance marketplace can bring in your first clients while you build a client list of your own.

Over the years, what a hustle earns can grow into savings that pay you on their own. So whichever you start with, set aside the tax on each payment and move a fixed share of the rest into a low-cost index fund the day it arrives.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

Industry observers note that walt Disney World tickets and one-day Disneyland tickets cost less on slow dates, so pick your days on Disney’s price calendar before you book anything else. Buy from Disney or an authorized seller, pay for Lightning Lane passes to skip lines only on crowded days, and pack your own snacks and water.

Dates matter most at Walt Disney World, where a standard ticket’s price depends on the day it starts.

Industry observers note that A 3-day ticket for one park a day costs $589.38 for anyone 10 or older if it starts Dec. 26, 2027, and $410.47 if it starts Sept. 12, 2027. For four people that age, the September dates save $715.64 before tax.

Disneyland prices only its one-day tickets by date, from $104 to $224. Its multi-day tickets cost the same on any date, and each day you add lowers the daily price, from $167.50 on a 2-day ticket for anyone 10 or older to $104 on a 5-day one.

According to recent reports, buy from Disney or an authorized seller. A cheap ticket from a stranger may be fake, and even a real one can be canceled, since Disney’s rules tie each ticket to one person for all its days.

Then weigh each extra on its own instead of buying it by default:.

If you carry the Disney Visa Card, Disney Premier Visa Card, or Disney Inspire Visa Card, pay with it in the parks for its discounts on select meals and merchandise.

Before you settle on dates, check the lowest-price link on Disney World’s ticket calendar, which names the cheapest months for the ticket length you choose.

To price your own dates, open Disney’s theme park tickets page and pick the resort you’ll visit.

#56519. Latest Update: Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

📅 13 Oct 2024 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1988 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

📅 13 Oct 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.
  • As Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs.
  • But out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.

As Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs. Trump should not be consuming much of our time. Sure, we do our research and cast our votes but after that we move right on to focus on other things within our own circle of control.

But out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money. Your money, the economy in general, and the overall wealth of the nation.

According to recent reports, politicians are already not known for being the sharpest tools in the shed when it comes to technical stuff like science, technology, or economics. But this year the discourse has become particularly dumb, as our candidates try to manipulate undecided voters in swing states with ideas that are based on irrational emotions rather than sound economic sense.

For one particularly funny example, you may have noticed that the competing party (Trump in this case) is attacking the incumbents (Biden/Harris) over the “bad economy.” When in fact the US economy is stronger than it has ever been, with the lowest unemployment we’ve ever seen as well.

It’s hard to imagine a better situation than we have right now, and in fact the recent bout of higher inflation is a sign that things have been going too well, and we needed to step on the brakes with the help of higher interest rates.

But somehow the people still seem to believe that we have a “bad” economy. Take a look at this Gallup poll showing that while most people (85%) are doing really well right now, they assume that it’s just their own good fortune – only 17% believe the economy is doing well.

This is mathematically impossible, because if most people are doing well, that’s the definition of a good economy! And suspiciously enough, this widespread wrongness correlates quite nicely with the rise of social media misinformation.

In a recent development, so the politicians and the news have been doing the opposite of what they should be doing in an ideal situation (sharing accurate information). And sure, we can always just ignore their speeches and go on with our lives. But when it comes to economics, knowledge is power (and money). The more accurately we understand how things really work, the wealthier we will all become.

So with all that in mind, I hereby present you with my list of the….

Top Dumb Things Politicians Want You To Believe About The Economy.

1: The President Controls the Economy.

If there’s a recession, the opposition party likes to blame it on the current president. If the economy is booming, the current president likes to give himself (or possibly soon herself) credit for all of that success. But really, the US economy is way too massive – and thankfully way too free – for the president to control or really even influence all that strongly.

In reality, our economy is a gigantic machine which converts labor and materials into things like iPhones, hospitals and pumpkin pies. And although we’re the biggest economy at 26% of the planet, we are still heavily influenced by that much bigger 74% of economic activity that the other 7.6 billion people on Earth are busy producing everywhere else.

When we have our inevitable little boom and bust cycles, they are mostly caused by the normal cycle of irrational exuberance (and greed) like the 2007 housing boom, followed by brief periods of extreme fear and pessimism like the 2008-2012 financial and housing crash.

The government does play a role too, by setting tax rates and other rules. But the effects of these policies are usually so delayed and unpredictable, that you can’t draw a straight line between today’s president and today’s economy. In other words, the government does its best to adjust the rudder on our giant ship, but in the short term our economy lurches around on the waves and storms of the ocean.

2: The President Controls Interest Rates.

Recent findings suggest that this one is especially funny to me, as our candidates feign sympathy for the hard life of middle class Americans, who now face higher borrowing costs on their credit cards and car loans and mortgages. They claim they will fight to bring the interest rates down. Trump even goes as far as bullying our Federal Reserve board members (who can only do their jobs if we allow them to function as independent experts) and suggesting that he would take over the whole department, if elected.

In a recent development, the real story is that while monetary policy would be a terrible tool to leave in the hands of a sitting president (see Argentina), it does function as an excellent set of gas and brake pedals for the economy if used properly. When things slow down and unemployment gets too high, a cut to the interest rates will produce a boost in everything from latest jobs to stock prices. But if things get too hot, you get rapid inflation which can mess up the system.

3: Inflation has Made Life Harder for Americans (and the President Can Magically Reverse it).

It has been revealed that this line of reasoning is even dumber than the last one. For a couple of years after the Covid era, we had rapid inflation. It was caused by a rare combination of a goods shortage caused by things like factory closures and remote work, plentiful demand from government stimulus spending and low interest rates. These factors have since ironed themselves out, and inflation is back down to an ultra-low 2.4%.

But most significantly, wages have still risen faster than inflation so we are all better off than before! Since 2019, overall prices are up 19% and our wages are up 21%. So even after all that inflation, we are still doing just fine. But the candidates are still bickering over inflation as if it’s an actual problem, and even worse promising to “bring prices back down”. And they’ve managed to convince the electorate that “higher wages and prices” is the same thing as “a bad economy”. Which is just plain wrong.

Industry observers note that bonus dumbness: politicians also occasionally blame “greedy corporations” for increasing prices to hoard profits. While price increases are totally acceptable in a market system (as a business owner you are free to set prices wherever you like), in reality it doesn’t usually happen because our markets are too competitive. For example, a recent deep analysis from NPR highlighted that no, grocery stores haven’t made any windfall profit at all off of this recent bout of Covid-fueled inflation.

4: The President Controls Housing Prices.

One key thing that has changed over the past ten years is that US house prices and rents have both risen much faster than general inflation and even wages. On the positive side, interest rates have also risen which tends to make houses feel more expensive and is supposed to help bring house prices down. But it hasn’t happened yet which means we have the double whammy of higher prices and higher interest costs for mortgage borrowers.

The dumb part is that our candidates are proposing things that would make the problem even worse, like subsidies for first-time homebuyers or schemes to reduce the interest rates. When really the solution is to increase the supply of housing, which I personally think will happen if we stop putting up roadblocks for homebuilders (myself included) to build housing.

Things like faster and cheaper permits, less onerous and expensive building codes, eliminating suburban-style zoning and setback and car parking rules, and changing laws so that NIMBYs no longer get any say over what other people do with their own land could all help reduce the cost of building a house by about 50%, quickly and permanently.

5: The President Controls Gas Prices, and They Are Presently “High” and We Want Them Lower.

It has been revealed that ahh, gasoline! The most ridiculous of things to worry about and the fuel for many of MMM’s rants since 2011.

First of all, on an inflation-adjusted basis, gasoline is still about the same price as it was in 1950: in the $3-4 range per gallon, in today’s dollars.

Secondly, it is so cheap that even with our huge inefficient American vehicles, the average household is still only spending 2.5% of their disposable income on the stuff! (The funny part is that they spend many times more on the rest of the car ownership experience while thinking gas is the part that is expensive).

Third, gasoline has been obsolete for almost a decade now. You can get a used electric car for less than the price of a comparable used gas car, or if you’re a fancypants money waster like me, newly introduced EVs are also cheaper than their gas counterparts. You get a faster, nicer car that almost never needs maintenance OR gasoline, and save money.

So why are we even still talking about this antique fuel of a previous era? Why aren’t the candidates also arguing over the price of Kodak film or typewriters or fax machines?

6: The Economy is Something We Should Even Worry About.

Industry observers note that the funniest part about all this economic talk is that we’re focusing on the wrong thing. While hard work and business and advancing the frontiers of human knowledge are all fun things, the reality is that we passed the point of having “Enough” decades ago. When the American middle class complains about how hard we have it these days, it’s like a bunch of overfed people at a buffet wishing they could just have one more flavor of donuts stacked onto the table.

Yes, we have income and wealth inequality so that the rich tend to get richer more quickly. And yes, we should keep that in check with a somewhat progressive tax system because a more equal society tends to be a more peaceful and happy one.

But have you noticed that as the rich people get richer, they don’t get any happier? It’s because after you pass the point of “Enough”, adding more money doesn’t really help much.

And “Enough” is much more defined by your mindset (and your collection of life skills) than your paycheck. So if the politicians really cared about improving our happiness and wellbeing, they’d be preaching the Principles of Mustachianism rather than pandering to the specific requests of coal miners or billionaires.

According to recent reports, but alas, winning an election is a very different thing than proposing stuff that is actually best for the country. And for that reason, we cast our votes for the best party and then tune back out until the next election.

In the Comments: Has the election season been getting you down, pumping you up, or just giving you a thorough dose of “Meh”?

It has been revealed that while researching economic stats for this article, I came across a quirky but informative series of videos called USA Facts by none other than former Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer. It seems that he had the same frustration as me: Americans are fighting over a bunch of opinions and misinformation without even bothering to look up the actual facts. So he made a well-produced series of videos that just share the facts without the baggage of political hype on top of them. I wish our politicians could do the same thing!

In a recent development, ask each DJ to quote the reception alone, without the ceremony or cocktail hour, so you pay only for the hours you need a DJ. At a small wedding, a playlist on rented speakers can do the DJ’s job, with a confident friend on the microphone for the entrances and toasts.

Before you sign with anyone, settle four details:.

Real Estate Notes Make You the Lender – Check the Collateral Before You Lend

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (434 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A real estate note lets you lend against someone else’s property and collect the interest.
  • The property is your protection, but only if you can claim it and sell it for at least what you’re owed.
  • You can buy a performing note, one whose borrower is paying, or pay less than the loan’s balance for a non-performing note, one whose borrower has stopped paying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A real estate note lets you lend against someone else’s property and collect the interest. Before you put money in, confirm your loan is no more than 70% of the property’s appraised value and gets repaid first if the property sells. If you can’t check that yourself, spread small amounts across many loans.

The interest is the appeal. The property is your protection, but only if you can claim it and sell it for at least what you’re owed.

You can buy a performing note, one whose borrower is paying, or pay less than the loan’s balance for a non-performing note, one whose borrower has stopped paying. You can lend straight to a house flipper. Or you can buy slices of many loans through a real estate crowdfunding platform. The real estate bonds some apps sell are loans to the company itself and give you no claim on a particular property.

A default can end in foreclosure, and foreclosures are slow. Homes foreclosed in the second quarter of 2026 had spent an average of 563 days in the process, according to property data firm ATTOM. Texas averaged 155 days and Fresh York 2,007. You can’t cash out early, either. You get your money back as the borrower repays, or by finding someone to buy the note.

Before you buy a note or lend directly, check five things:.

Say you lend $100,000 at 10% to a flipper on a house worth $160,000. You collect $10,000 a year until the project stalls and the payments stop. Then you pay a lawyer and keep up the property’s taxes and insurance until the foreclosure ends and the house sells. The $60,000 between the loan and the value has to cover those costs and any drop in price.

Unless you can run all five checks on every loan, spread the same $100,000 across 50 loans of $2,000 each, so one default puts a fiftieth of your money at risk instead of all of it.

Find a platform that sells slices of many loans among the best real estate crowdfunding sites.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that managing your money isn’t just about earning more. It’s also about stopping unnecessary losses. In today’s digital economy, recurring subscription charges (streaming services, premium apps, trials, memberships) quietly drain money each month. Most people spend hundreds, or even thousands, annually on services they don’t use. Subscription manager apps help you see recurring charges, track billing cycles, and cancel those you no longer want.

Before choosing an app, know what features matter most:.

Industry observers note that rocket Money is one of the most well-known subscription managers. It scans your linked bank and credit accounts for recurring charges and displays them on a clear dashboard. People like it for its ability to detect subscriptions and assist with cancellations directly in the app, a major time-saver for busy people.

Why it stands out• Automatically detects recurring payments• Lets you cancel unwanted subscriptions directly from the app• Includes extra budgeting tools and spending alerts• Trusted security with read-only bank access.

Who it’s for: People who want the fastest way to spot and stop unwanted recurring charges without manually entering every service.

Trim is another financial assistant that scans transactions and flags recurring charges. While subscription tracking is a smaller part of its feature set, it also provides bill negotiation support and money-saving alerts. Many users like Trim because it reaches out on your behalf about subscriptions via text or in-app messaging.

Why it stands out• Recurring transaction detection• Alerts about unusual subscriptions or trials converting to paid• Bill negotiation tools beyond basic subscription tracking.

Who it’s for: Users who want automation plus help reducing bills and optimizing spending.

Sources indicate that pocketGuard is primarily a budgeting app that includes subscription tracking as part of a broader financial overview. Instead of being solely a subscription manager, it integrates recurring expenses into your overall budget, helping you get a full picture of your finances.

Why it stands out• Syncs automatically with financial accounts• Highlights recurring expenses in the context of your whole budget• Helps track cash flow and affordability.

Who it’s for: People who want subscriptions tracked inside a complete personal finance dashboard.

Monarch Money offers robust financial planning tools: budgets, goals, net worth tracking, and more, with subscription visibility included in the package. Consumers often choose it for its highly customizable interface and deep analytics. It’s not subscription-only, but it gives you full clarity on recurring expenses as part of larger planning.

Why it stands out• Powerful budgeting + subscription tracking.• Clean, customizable data visuals.• Goal-based money management.

Who it’s for: Users who want subscription insights in the context of total financial planning — and who are okay paying for premium features.

Sources indicate that if you don’t want to link bank accounts, Bobby is a lightweight subscription tracker that lets you manually enter each subscription, along with billing dates and amounts. It then sends reminders so you don’t forget renewals. It’s simple, privacy-friendly, and great for a hands-on approach.

Why it stands out• No bank/credit card linking required.• Clean and minimal interface.• Calendar views and notification reminders.

Who it’s for: Privacy-focused customers or those who prefer full manual control.

Recent findings suggest that subby offers functionality similar to Bobby’s but is known for integrations and subscription reminders tailored for Android users. It lets you manually track expenses with flexible billing schedules and alerts. (While not all resources list Subby as a top pick, it’s frequently mentioned among good manual trackers.).

Why it stands out• Manual entry with customizable notifications.• Good choice for Android customers.

Who it’s for: People who want a simple manual tracker without linking financial accounts.

If you’d rather not use a third-party app at all, both Apple and Google offer direct subscription management:.

iPhone (Apple Subscriptions):Settings → Your Name → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel Subscription.

Android (Google Play):Open Google Play → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel subscription.

These built-in tools won’t automatically find all recurring charges if some are billed outside the app stores, but they are a secure and effective way to manage many mobile subscriptions.

Here’s a quick guide based on what matters most to you:.

You can also combine approaches — use a subscription app plus your budgeting system to spot recurring leaks and strategy better for annual vs monthly charges.

Subscription manager apps help plug the leaks in your financial bucket, so more of your hard-earned money stays where it belongs: with you. Whether you want automatic detection and help with cancellations, a full financial overview, or full privacy with manual entry, there’s an option that fits your style. Explore one or two subscription manager apps that align with your priorities, and don’t forget to check your finances regularly.

Almost 70% of people turning 65 will need long-term care, meaning help with bathing, dressing, and other daily tasks, according to the Administration for Community Living. One in five will need it for more than five years.

Recent findings suggest that your age and health set what insurance costs and whether you can buy it. Most individual long-term care policies require a health review, so a diagnosis in your 60s can raise your price or rule you out.

In a recent development, the American Association for Long-Term Care Insurance’s 2026 price index demonstrates a couple, both 55, paying about $5,000 a year combined, on average. That buys each of them a policy whose care benefits start at $165,000 and grow 3% a year. At 65, the same coverage averages about $7,000 a year.

Industry observers note that start by looking up typical prices in your area with CareScout’s cost of care calculator. Nationally, CareScout’s 2025 survey puts an in-home caregiver 44 hours a week at $80,080 a year, assisted living at $74,400, and a private nursing home room at $129,575.

Talk with your family, too, about who would give care and whether you’d stay in your own home or move to a facility. Ask your parents the same questions about their own care.

Industry observers note that get quotes for both kinds from an independent agent who sells several insurers’ policies. Identical coverage for an Illinois couple, both 60, ranged from $4,591 to $7,173 a year across five insurers in the same price index.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you live within about 10 miles of work and have a safe route, bike there two or three days a week instead of driving. Each day you ride saves gas, car upkeep, and any parking fee, so a used bike and basic gear can pay for themselves within a year where you pay to park.

Every mile you bike instead of driving saves about 29 cents, AAA’s 2026 average for a newly introduced car’s gas, maintenance, repairs, and tires.

You don’t have to ride every day for the savings to add up. Say you live 6 miles from work, about a 30-minute ride, and bike there three days a week for 50 weeks. You’d otherwise pay $5 a day to park, and the bike needs about $150 a year in tune-ups and flat repairs. Those rides take 1,800 miles off the car, worth about $520 at 29 cents a mile, and skip $750 in parking, so you keep roughly $1,100 after upkeep.

With $1,100 a year in savings, $500 spent on a used bike, lights, a helmet, a sturdy lock, and a rain jacket pays for itself in under six months. After a year, you’re about $600 ahead. Where parking at work is free, you keep about $370 a year, and the same gear takes about 16 months to pay for itself. The six rides also give you three hours of exercise a week.

According to recent reports, keep the ride to about 10 miles each way, or ride to a train or bus for part of a longer trip. An e-bike lets you ride farther, but it often costs $1,000 to $4,000. Portland State University researchers track the state and city programs that help pay for one, and some give lower-income buyers $1,000 or more.

Before your first commute, test the route on a weekend. Pick bike lanes and quiet streets over the fastest roads, and leave a change of clothes at work.

Recent findings suggest that then ask HR what your employer offers bike commuters, such as a bike room, showers, or a taxable stipend. A carpool or a remote day can cut your commuting costs the rest of the week.

Ride the route you tested one day next week, then add a day each week until you’re riding three.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that managing money as a household is harder than it looks. Most people use a regular checking account at a massive bank, then juggle a separate budgeting app, maybe a savings account somewhere else, and possibly a kids’ debit card on top of that. It’s a lot to keep track of.

Crew is a fintech app that tries to put all of that in one place. It combines a high-yield checking account, built-in budgeting tools, and family banking features – all inside a single app. The goal is to help you organize your money, automate your budget, and earn more interest without switching between apps.

In this Crew review, we cover what it is, how it works, who it’s best for, the key features, pricing, and what real consumers are saying. If you’re looking for a smarter checking account that does more, this review gives you the full picture.

Crew is a fintech app that tries to put all of that in one place. It combines a high-yield checking account, built-in budgeting tools, and family banking features.

• High-yield checking • Debit cards available for kids• Unlimited budgeting pockets• Cash deposits and mobile check deposit• No monthly fees or minimum balances.

• App-only banking with no desktop login• No physical check writing.

Crew is a financial technology (fintech) company based in Lehi, Utah. It was founded by Gentry Davies and Steve Domino, who previously worked at Divvy, a business expense platform acquired by Bill.com. The app debuted publicly and has been growing steadily since 2023.

Crew is not a bank. Banking services are provided by Bangor Savings Bank, which is FDIC-insured. Your deposits are held at Bangor Savings Bank, so they are protected up to federal insurance limits – $250,000 for individual accounts and $500,000 for joint accounts.

Sources indicate that the app is available on both iOS and Android. A web app is currently in beta.

Crew works well for a wide range of people, but it’s especially useful if you fall into one of these groups:.

Crew may not be the right fit for:.

According to recent reports, crew offers a checking account that earns 2.95% APY on your full balance. This rate applies to every dollar you hold in the account – there’s no minimum deposit requirement and no tiered rate structure.

Why it matters: Most significant bank checking accounts pay close to 0.01% APY. Earning nearly 3% on your everyday checking balance can add meaningful interest over time, especially for families keeping a few thousand dollars in their account at any given time.

Pockets are virtual “buckets” inside your single Crew checking account. You can create as many as you need – for example, one for bills, one for savings, one for a vacation fund, one for groceries.

Sources indicate that why it matters: You don’t need a separate savings account or multiple bank accounts. Pockets let you visually and mentally divide your money without moving it to another institution. You can also lock a pocket in “piggy bank mode” to avoid dipping into it.

Crew’s Autopilot feature lets you create rules that move money automatically based on triggers. Triggers can be events like a paycheck arriving or a balance dropping below a set level, or they can be time-based, like every Friday or the 1st of the month.

In a recent development, why it matters: Automation removes the discipline requirement from budgeting. You set your rules once, and Crew handles the rest. For example, you can tell Crew to automatically send 10% of every paycheck to your giving pocket, $500 to bills, and keep the rest in checking — without touching the app every payday.

Why it matters: Most banking apps bolt on a kid’s account as an afterthought. Crew builds family banking into the core experience. Parents get real-time spending notifications, spend controls, and the ability to set automated allowances.

Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

📅 16 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1490 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.
  • Industry observers note that “I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers.
  • In a recent development, so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

I thought to myself at the time,.

Industry observers note that “I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”.

In a recent development, so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!).

Recent findings suggest that among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore new places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

Industry observers note that with all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

It has been revealed that while my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the significant-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.).

Sources indicate that this level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

According to recent reports, as we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

In summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a fresh cost too since I was self-insured back then.

Sources indicate that my budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

This strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible initiative ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze plan in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

Recent findings suggest that but as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

When it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which says that,.

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

Industry observers note that for me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

The only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I at the moment live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out. I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

But I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

According to recent reports, in the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

But for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

Make these changes before your next trip.

Give Your Budget a Fun-Money Line So One Splurge Doesn’t End It

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that build a set amount of fun money into your budget each pay period, and spend it on anything you like with no tracking and no guilt.
  • According to recent reports, A budget that bans every treat works like a crash diet.
  • It has been revealed that sort your budget’s lines, the categories you give money to, into two kinds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that build a set amount of fun money into your budget each pay period, and spend it on anything you like with no tracking and no guilt. Fund savings, bills, and debt payments first, so a splurge never comes out of them. Room for small pleasures is what keeps you from quitting your budget.

According to recent reports, A budget that bans every treat works like a crash diet. It holds for a few weeks until one splurge makes the whole blueprint feel broken, and you quit.

It has been revealed that sort your budget’s lines, the categories you give money to, into two kinds. Firm lines are savings transfers, bills, and debt payments, and you never borrow from them. Flexible lines, such as groceries, dining out, and clothes, can change from month to month. Fun money is a flexible line too, and the only one with no rules about what it buys.

In a recent development, once treats have their own line, buying one stops feeling like a failure. A $12 lunch paid from the fun line is spending you planned, so there’s nothing to hide from your budget or make up for later.

Fund the firm lines first, then set the fun line at 5% to 10% of take-home pay. While you’re paying off a credit card or other high-interest debt, keep it closer to 5%. If you and a partner combine finances, set a separate amount for each of you, so neither has to justify a purchase.

Keep the fun money in a separate free checking account with its own debit card, so the balance is all you ever check. Say you’re paid twice a month and take home $3,500 a month. Moving $150 from each paycheck into that account gives you $300 a month to spend on anything, a little under 9% of take-home pay.

Sources indicate that cover any overspending that month by moving money from another flexible line, the same move a zero-based budget uses to keep every dollar assigned. Never take it from savings. If the same line runs over three months in a row, its amount is too low for how you live, so raise it and trim another flexible line by the same amount.

Choose your amount before your next payday, and set up an automatic transfer so it reaches the fun-money account the same day your pay arrives.

What Is Dollar Cost Averaging?

📅 07 May 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone.
  • Dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table.
  • In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone. A lot of people hold back because they are afraid of buying at the wrong time.

Dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table. Instead of trying to time the market perfectly, you invest a fixed amount on a regular schedule and let time do the heavy lifting.

In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.

Recent findings suggest that dollar cost averaging (DCA) is an investment strategy in which you invest a fixed dollar amount in a specific asset at regular intervals, regardless of market conditions. Whether the market is up, down, or flat, you invest the same amount on the same schedule.

It has been revealed that the result is that you end up buying more shares when prices are low and fewer shares when prices are high. Over time, this can lower your average cost per share compared to making a single lump-sum investment at the wrong moment.

In a recent development, most people already practice dollar cost averaging without realizing it. If you contribute to a 401(k) every time you get a paycheck, that is dollar cost averaging in action.

The mechanics are straightforward. You pick an investment, decide on a fixed dollar amount, and choose a schedule. Every week, every two weeks, or every month, you invest that amount, no matter what the market is doing that day.

Industry observers note that because you are investing a fixed dollar amount rather than a fixed number of shares, your money automatically buys more shares when prices dip and fewer when prices climb. This built-in dynamic is what makes the strategy so useful for investors who want to build wealth steadily without spending hours watching the market.

Recent findings suggest that for most people, low-cost index funds are the best vehicle for this strategy. They give you broad diversification across hundreds of companies in a single investment, and their expense ratios are far lower than actively managed mutual funds or target-date funds. That difference in fees compounds significantly over decades.

Industry observers note that say you decide to invest $300 every month into a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. Here is what three months might look like:.

After three months, you have invested $900 and own 21 shares. Your average cost per share is $42.86. If you had invested all $900 in Month 1 at $50 per share, you would only own 18 shares. The dip in Month 2 actually worked in your favor because you had cash ready to put to work at a lower price.

This is the core idea. You stop worrying about whether today is a good day to invest and start focusing on building a consistent habit instead.

It removes emotion from investing.

One of the biggest mistakes investors make is letting fear and excitement drive their decisions. They pile in when the market is hot and pull out when it drops. Dollar-cost averaging sidesteps all of that by turning investing into a routine, like paying a bill, that runs automatically on a schedule.

It makes market downturns work for you.

When markets fall, most people panic. With dollar cost averaging, a dip is simply an opportunity to buy more shares at a discount. If you stay consistent, you will naturally accumulate more of your investment when it is on sale.

It is accessible no matter your income.

According to recent reports, you do not need a large lump sum to get started. Even small, consistent contributions can grow meaningfully over time thanks to compounding. A good starting point is to aim for at least 10% of your gross income going toward investments. If that feels like a stretch right now, start with whatever you can manage and increase it over time.

Consistency is the real edge in personal investing. Dollar cost averaging encourages exactly that. When you automate your contributions, investing happens in the background while you get on with your life.

Industry observers note that want a free tool to help you keep track of your investments? Check out Empower!

Dollar cost averaging is a sound strategy, but it is worth understanding its limits before you dive in.

If you are investing in a low-quality asset that trends downward over time, buying it consistently will not save you. That is why what you invest in matters just as much as how you invest. Sticking to broad, low-cost index funds gives you exposure to the overall market rather than betting on a single manufacturer’s performance. Investing heavily in individual stocks introduces a level of risk that most people do not need to take on.

Alternative investments should stay small.

Sources indicate that things like gold, cryptocurrency, and other alternative assets can have a place in a portfolio, but they should stay well under 10% of your total invested assets. These assets tend to be far more volatile and speculative than a diversified index fund, and there is no reason to let them dominate your long-term strategy.

A lump sum can outperform in a rising market.

According to recent reports, research has shown that if you have a large sum ready to invest, putting it all in at once tends to outperform dollar cost averaging over the long run, simply because markets go up more often than they go down. That said, most people do not have a large lump sum sitting around. For those building wealth paycheck by paycheck, dollar cost averaging is the practical and sensible path.

Getting started with dollar cost averaging does not require a financial advisor or a complicated setup. Here is a simple framework:.

Dollar cost averaging is one of the most practical investing strategies available to everyday investors. It takes the guesswork out of market timing, helps you build a consistent habit, and naturally positions you to benefit from market dips over time.

Industry observers note that the key is to pair this strategy with the right investments. Low-cost index funds are a strong foundation. They offer diversification, keep fees low, and have a long track record of rewarding patient investors. Avoid concentrating too much on single stocks or speculative alternatives, and keep contributing regularly regardless of what the market is doing on any given day.

If you stay the course and keep contributing, time becomes your greatest asset.

In a recent development, to pay less for concert and theater tickets, buy early through artist and credit card presales, or late through theater lotteries, rush lines, and resale listings for reveals that aren’t sold out. Before you buy resale, compare the all-in price across sites, which sellers now have to show up front.

Brokers using bots can buy many tickets the moment they go on sale, a 2018 Government Accountability Office report found, so fans often pay a reseller’s markup. In the events it sampled, fees averaged 27% of the ticket price on the original sale and 31% on resale.

The cheapest seats usually sell at the start of a sale or close to the show. A presale lets you buy at face value, the price before fees, ahead of the general public. In a show’s final days, theaters release discounted seats, and resellers with tickets to a show that isn’t sold out often cut prices.

Most Broadway shows, and some tours, run a digital lottery, a drawing for discounted seats. Enter through the show’s website, Broadway Direct, or the TodayTix app. Say a hit show’s seats cost $250 and its lottery price is $49. Win a pair and you pay $98 instead of $500, in seats the box office picks. Discounted rush tickets go on sale the morning of the show, and some theaters sell standing room once a performance sells out. TKTS booths in Newly introduced York and Philadelphia sell same-day seats for up to 50% off. TDF, the nonprofit that runs them, also sells a $42-a-year membership that lets those who qualify, such as retirees and people 30 and under, buy Broadway tickets for $53.50 to $62.50.

It has been revealed that compare resale prices for the same seats on Ticketmaster, StubHub, and SeatGeek. Since May 2025, a Federal Trade Commission rule has required every seller, resale sites among them, to show the total price, mandatory fees included, up front.

It has been revealed that for a show that’s sure to sell out, the presale is your best shot at face value. For any other show, check resale again in its final days.

Taking a Second Job? Fix Your Withholding and Protect Your Main Job

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (485 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, before you take a second job, head off the three ways it can backfire.
  • Recent findings suggest that none of the three reveals up in your first week.
  • Each employer withholds tax as if its paycheck were your only income, unless your W-4, the form that sets your withholding, states otherwise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, before you take a second job, head off the three ways it can backfire. Have your main employer withhold extra tax to cover the second paycheck, check that employer’s rules on outside work, and set hours and an end date that protect your sleep and your main job.

Recent findings suggest that none of the three reveals up in your first week. The tax bill comes due when you file your return, and a broken work rule or exhaustion can take months to cost you.

Each employer withholds tax as if its paycheck were your only income, unless your W-4, the form that sets your withholding, states otherwise. On your return, the two incomes are taxed as one, so you usually owe more on the second job’s pay than its employer took out. Owing $1,000 or more when you file can also bring an IRS underpayment penalty.

The other two put your main job, the bigger of your two paychecks, at risk.

To fix the tax, start the newly introduced job with a W-4 that has only your personal details and signature. After its first payday, run the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator, which needs a recent pay stub from each job. The extra withholding it finds goes on the W-4 for your higher-paying job, so give your main employer an updated one.

Recent findings suggest that protecting your main job starts before you apply. Read your employer’s handbook and any contract you signed. Some employers require approval for outside work, a conflict-of-interest rule can bar a job with a client or vendor, and a noncompete agreement can bar one with a competitor. When you interview, offer the same hours every week, such as weekends from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., so the fresh shifts never overlap your main job.

Cap the hours so you still sleep at least seven hours a night, the minimum the CDC recommends for adults. Give the job a goal, too. Say a teacher works 12 weekend hours at a bike shop for $20 an hour and loses 30% to taxes. That leaves about $730 a month, enough to clear a $6,000 credit card balance at 22% interest in about nine months. Then the teacher quits.

The extra pay is worth it only while your main job stays safe, so put your end date on your calendar before the first shift.
